source: Cox & D'Antonio 3e Table C.3, PDF pages 549-552 (printed pp. 492-495)
about:
The twenty-seven surfaces of Table C.3, "2D BEM predictions", print over four pages, sideways on the page. Twenty-six of them take three printed lines each, one per angle of incidence, headed 0, 56.9 and Random; the first takes one line, "Plane surfaces, non-absorbing, any size", whose angle column reads "All/any" and whose eighteen cells are all 0.00. The columns are the one-third octave bands from 100 Hz to 5 kHz, and the values are correlation scattering coefficients, dimensionless. Every cell is filled.

Section 5.3.7 (PDF page 222, printed p. 165) says this table "considers single-plane diffusers but predicted using a 2D BEM" and that "the table includes all the surfaces included in the diffusion coefficient table, except hybrid surfaces", which is why its numbered sections run 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 with no section 6: section 6 of Appendix B is the hybrid surfaces. The same section states two limits of the data in the book's own words: "the random incidence coefficients tend to have raised values at low frequencies, especially for deep surfaces; values of up to 0.2 at 100 Hz are calculated for many surfaces", for which "a pragmatic solution would be to set all scattering coefficients to 0 for frequencies where a quarter wavelength is larger than the surface depth"; and, on the next page (PDF page 223, printed p. 166), that "the scattering coefficient does not discriminate between different diffusers in a consistent manner", since "the coefficient also interprets redirection as scattering. For instance, a 45 degree triangle returns a strong reflection back to a normal source, as discussed in Chapter 11, yet the scattering coefficient interprets this as dispersion".

Section 13.3.8 (PDF page 512, printed p. 455) adds what a modeller has to do with them: "the 2D predictions in Table C.3 are for the plane of maximum scattering, whereas most diffuse reflection algorithms will interpret these values as being for hemispherically scattering devices and distribute the scattered energy according to Lambert's law. So, although the predictions were produced using single-plane scatterers, they will probably be better matched to hemispherical scatterers in many GRAMs."

The surfaces are the ones of Appendix B and the descriptions are not always spelled the same way in the two tables. Appendix B opens its width series with "1 period, 0.61 cm wide" where this table prints "1 period, 0.61 m wide", which is the errata entry the width belongs to; Appendix B prints "4 cylinders, 2.44 m wide" where this table prints "4 periods, 2.44 m wide"; and Appendix B prints "30 cm deep (semicylinders)" where this table prints the singular. The values are the same where the surface is.

That surface is listed twice here as it is there: "6 periods, 3.66 m wide" of section 1 and "30 cm deep (semicylinder)" of section 2 carry the same fifty-four values across all three angles, because six semicylinders of radius 0.3 m spanning 3.66 m is one object read into two series.

not_derivable.angle_of_incidence_deg: the page prints “All/any” in that column: a plane surface scatters nothing at any angle, so the row stands for all of them
